title: How to Apply for a Mayor's Permit / Business Permit
description: Secure your local license to operate a business within your city or municipality.

requirements.title: DTI/SEC Registration
requirements.description: Proof of business name or entity registration.

requirements.title: Barangay Clearance
requirements.description: Local clearance from the barangay where the business is located.

requirements.title: Lease Contract
requirements.description: Proof of business address or occupancy.

requirements.title: Valid ID
requirements.description: Government-issued ID of the business owner or representative.

requirements.title: Cedula
requirements.description: Community Tax Certificate of the applicant.

checklist.title: Secure Initial Docs
checklist.description: Obtain your DTI or SEC registration and local barangay clearance.

checklist.title: Submit Application
checklist.description: File your business permit application at the City or Municipal Hall's BPLO.

checklist.title: Undergo Inspections
checklist.description: Prepare for required inspections by the fire, sanitation, and zoning departments.

checklist.title: Pay Fees
checklist.description: Settle the assessed taxes and permit fees at the LGU cashier.

checklist.title: Claim Permit
checklist.description: Receive your Mayor's Permit and business plate for display at your establishment.

content.title: What is Mayor's Permit / Business Permit?

blocks.content: A Mayor's Permit, also called a Business Permit, is an official authorization issued by the Local Government Unit (LGU) allowing a business to legally operate within a city or municipality in the Philippines.
Businesses are generally required to secure a Mayor's Permit before starting operations and renew it annually.

The Mayor's Permit is commonly used for:
* Legal operation of businesses
* BIR and tax compliance
* Opening business bank accounts
* Applying for government accreditations and contracts

You may need a Mayor's Permit if you are:
- Starting a sole proprietorship, partnership, or corporation
- Operating a physical store, office, or commercial establishment
- Running an online business with local operations
- Renewing an existing business annually

blocks.title: Legal Authority to Operate
blocks.content: The permit allows businesses to legally conduct operations within the jurisdiction of the LGU.

blocks.title: Compliance with Government Regulations
blocks.content: It demonstrates compliance with local ordinances, zoning, sanitation, and safety requirements.

blocks.title: Required for Other Business Transactions
blocks.content: Banks, suppliers, and government agencies often require a valid business permit.
Most Mayor's Permit applications are processed through the Business Permits and Licensing Office (BPLO) of the city or municipality where the business is located.

blocks.title: Online Application
blocks.content:
Some LGUs provide:
* Online appointment systems
* Electronic submission portals
* Online payment options
Availability depends on the local government unit.

blocks.title: Walk-In Application
blocks.content:
Applicants may personally visit the BPLO to:
* Submit requirements
* Undergo inspections
* Pay fees
* Claim permits
**Pro Tip:** Use the BIR **eFPS or eBIRForms** for faster filing and avoid manual queuing at the RDO. Most payments can now be done via GCash or Maya.

blocks.title: Secure Preliminary Business Documents
blocks.content:
Prepare your:
* DTI or SEC registration
* Barangay Clearance
* Lease contract or proof of address
* Valid IDs and other supporting documents

blocks.title: Submit the Business Permit Application
blocks.content: Submit the application form and documentary requirements to the BPLO.
The office will review your application and assess fees.

blocks.title: Undergo Inspections
blocks.content:
Depending on the business type, inspections may be conducted by:
* Fire Department
* Sanitation Office
* Engineering Office
* Zoning Office

blocks.title: Pay the Assessed Fees
blocks.content:
Pay the required taxes and permit fees at:
* City Hall cashier
* Authorized payment centers
* Online LGU payment portals
Keep all official receipts.

blocks.title: Claim the Mayor's Permit
blocks.content:
After approval and payment verification, claim your:
* Mayor's Permit
* Business plate or sticker (if applicable)
* Official receipts and certificates
Display the permit prominently at your business establishment.

Applicants may process their Mayor's Permit at:
- City Hall Business Permits and Licensing Office (BPLO)
- Municipal Hall BPLO
- LGU online business portals
- Negosyo Centers (selected LGUs)
Applications are generally filed where the business establishment is physically located.

items: [City/Municipal Hall Website](https://www.gov.ph/services/lgu) (or visit your respective local city/municipal hall)

blocks.content:
Typical processing timelines include:
* Small businesses: 3–7 business days
* Businesses requiring inspections: 1–2 weeks
* Online renewal applications: Same day to 5 business days

Applicants may monitor their application through:
* BPLO inquiry counters
* LGU online portals
* SMS or email notifications (for participating LGUs)

Applicants may experience:
- Delayed inspections
- Incomplete documentary requirements
- Zoning or location issues
- Incorrect tax assessments
- Long queues during annual renewal season
Always review your application before final submission.

items: Apply early before peak renewal season
Bring multiple photocopies of all documents
Verify zoning compliance before leasing a location
Keep digital and printed copies of permits
Coordinate directly with your BPLO for updated requirements

blocks.title: Is a Mayor's Permit required for online businesses?
blocks.content: Yes, many LGUs require online businesses with local operations or inventory storage to secure permits.

blocks.title: How often should a Mayor's Permit be renewed?
blocks.content: Business permits are generally renewed annually, usually every January.

blocks.title: Can I operate without a Mayor's Permit?
blocks.content: Operating without a permit may result in penalties, closure orders, or fines from the LGU.

blocks.title: Is the process different for corporations?
blocks.content: Yes. Corporations and partnerships generally require SEC registration and additional documents.

blocks.title: What happens if I renew late?
blocks.content: Late renewal may result in penalties, surcharges, and additional interest charges.
